caption:
"It's fatigued" is the most common reason a good ad gets switched off. It's often the wrong diagnosis.

In Issue #5 of Decoded, Raj separates three kinds of fatigue that look identical in a dashboard: a tired opening, a saturated audience and a reason to buy that has stopped working. Only one of them means cut.

Also inside: why look-alike refreshes backfire (in Galvor's data, six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less first-month spend) and a ten-minute check to run before anyone hits pause.

# Decoded
by Galvor AI · Issue #5

Missed Issue #4? *Beyond Narrative*

---

## Creative fatigue: when to refresh, when to cut

*"It's fatigued" is the most common reason a good ad gets switched off. It's often the wrong diagnosis, and the fix is usually smaller than a new shoot.*

By Raj Dhakad, Founding AI Engineer, Galvor AI · Decoded by Galvor, Issue #5

### Key takeaways

- Fatigue has three causes, and each needs a different fix: the opening has worn out, the audience has seen it too often, or the reason to buy has stopped working. Only the last one means cut.
- Don't judge new ads too early. Galvor has seen some ad styles start about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and end close to average over their life.
- Refreshing with look-alikes doesn't work. In Galvor's data, six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less first-month spend.

## Monday, 9:40 a.m.

Sam's best ad, the kitchen-table founder video from Issue #4, is getting more expensive. Cost per order has crept up for ten days.

The agency's message arrives before Sam's coffee: "Creative fatigue. Recommend we pause and replace."

Sam has heard this before. Last time, they paused a winner, launched six fresh versions in a week, and spent a month getting back to where they started.

So this time Sam asks a different question: *what exactly is tired?*

## Three kinds of fatigue

When cost per order rises on a long-running ad, one of three things is usually happening. They look the same in a dashboard. They are not the same problem.

**1  The opening is tired**
- What it looks like: hook rate falls first. People who do watch past the opening still behave as before.
- What it means: the people seeing it have learned to scroll past the first frame. The rest of the ad still works.
- What to do: **refresh**. Recut the first three seconds; keep the middle and the CTA.

**2  The audience is saturated**
- What it looks like: frequency climbs, comments repeat, and the drop is spread across the whole ad.
- What it means: the ad hasn't stopped working. It has run out of new people of the type it speaks to.
- What to do: **shift**. Write for a new buyer (a different motivation, situation or objection) rather than a new look. Issue #3 explains why.

**3  The reason to buy has stopped working**
- What it looks like: people still watch, but fewer of them buy. Hold rate is steady; conversion falls.
- What it means: the offer, the claim or the moment has lost its pull, perhaps because a sale ended, the season changed or a competitor now says the same thing.
- What to do: **cut** this message, and test a new reason to buy.

Galvor's Actions use the same three words: Scale, Cut, Shift. Most ads called "fatigued" belong in the first two groups. Only the third is a reason to switch off.

## What Galvor saw in the data

Two findings from the last six months of ads Galvor analysed (new video ads launched May to September 2026) shape how we think about fatigue.

**New ads need time.** Galvor has seen some ad styles start about **35% dearer per order** in their first two months and end close to average over their life. Teams that compare a three-day-old replacement with a six-week-old winner are comparing a learner with a veteran. Judge new ads after weeks, not days.

**Look-alike refreshes hurt.** **Six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less first-month spend.** And new ads that looked like many running ads got **36% less**. Replacing one tired ad with six similar ones doesn't refresh anything. To Meta, it's the same ad split six ways.

[DATA NEEDED: median number of days from launch to the first sustained rise in CPO for top-spending ads, May–Sep 2026 set.]

[DATA NEEDED: of ads that showed rising CPO, the share where hook rate fell first vs hold rate vs conversion rate — to size each of the three causes.]

## What a refresh actually looks like

Back to Sam. When the team pulled the last 14 days apart, the answer was clear. Hook rate had fallen first. People who got past the opening still watched to the end and still bought at the same rate. The ad wasn't dead. Its first three seconds were.

So instead of a new shoot, the editor made three new openings for the same video:

- a customer's hand opening the product, instead of the founder holding it;
- a single line of on-screen text naming the buyer's problem;
- the proof moment, a customer message, moved to the very first frame.

Everything after second three stayed the same. Same founder, same kitchen table, same CTA.

This is the difference between a refresh and a replacement. A replacement throws away what the ad has already taught you and Meta. A refresh keeps the parts that still work and changes only the part that has worn out. It also makes the result readable: if one of the three openings brings hook rate back, you know exactly which attribute was tired.

There's a trap here too. Three new openings are three genuinely different first shots, not three colour grades of the same one. If the new openings all look alike, you're back to the look-alike problem from Issue #3.

[DATA NEEDED: for ads refreshed with a new opening only, how hook rate and CPO moved over the following 14 days vs ads that were fully replaced — anonymised.]

## Why "fatigue" gets diagnosed so often

Part of the reason is the dashboard. Cost per order is the number everyone watches, and it's the last number to move. By the time it rises, the cause happened days earlier, in a metric nobody was looking at.

Part of it is incentive. A replacement is visible work: new files, new shoots, a fresh batch of ads. A refresh looks small, even when it's the right call.

And part of it is memory. Without a record of how long your ads usually last, every rise in cost feels like the end. With one, you can tell a normal wobble from a real decline.

## A ten-minute fatigue check

Before anyone pauses an ad, answer these five questions with the ad set's last 14 days:

1. Which fell first: hook rate, hold rate or conversion rate?
2. Has frequency risen for the same audience?
3. Did anything change outside the ad: price, offer, stock, season?
4. Is the rise in cost steady, or one bad weekend?
5. What would replace it, and is that replacement genuinely new or a look-alike?

If you can't answer question 1, you can't diagnose fatigue yet. You can only feel it.

## The shift for marketers and leaders

Five moves Galvor recommends.

**1  Name the type of fatigue before you act**
Opening, audience or reason to buy. Each has a different fix. "Fatigue" on its own is not a diagnosis.

**2  Refresh the first three seconds before you replace the ad**
A new opening on a proven middle is hours of editing, not a new shoot, and it keeps what the ad has already taught Meta.

**3  Never refresh with look-alikes**
Replacing one ad with several near-copies in a few days splits the budget and teaches you nothing. One genuinely new ad beats six versions.

**4  Give replacements a fair test**
Use a test campaign with a set share of spend, and judge after weeks. Many styles start expensive and settle.

**5  Keep a fatigue log**
For every ad you pause, write one line: what fell first, what you changed and what happened next. In three months, that log will tell you how long your ads really last, and that's Brand Memory you can plan a budget on.

---
